title: Iran Just Hit US Bases in Kuwait and Bahrain. Millions of Indians in the Gulf Woke Up to Air-Raid Sirens.
excerpt: The ceasefire that was supposed to end the US-Iran war is in freefall. Iran launched missiles and drones at American military sites across the Gulf on Saturday, Trump threatened to erase Iran, and the Strait of Hormuz is being weaponised again.
body:
The ceasefire lasted twelve days.

On Saturday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched a coordinated wave of missiles and drones at US military facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain, the two Gulf states that host America's largest forward-deployed military presence in the region. Air-raid sirens wailed across Bahrain. Kuwait's air defences scrambled to intercept incoming projectiles.

The attacks came hours after President Donald Trump posted on social media that the US might be "forced to militarily complete the job," warning that if it came to that, "the Islamic Republic of Iran will no longer exist."

## How It Got Here

The US and Iran signed a 14-point interim agreement two weeks ago to halt four months of open warfare and reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. The deal was meant to buy time for deeper negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme and regional proxies.

It unravelled almost immediately.

On Thursday, an Iranian drone struck a Singapore-flagged cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz. The US responded with strikes on Iranian military targets — communications towers, air-defence systems, drone storage facilities and mine-laying capabilities across the port cities of Sirik and Bandar Lengeh and the island of Qeshm.

On Saturday, a second tanker was hit in the strait. Iran said the attacks were "warning shots" at vessels attempting to pass through routes not approved by Tehran. The Revolutionary Guards declared they would crack down harder on ships not seeking Iranian permits.

Then came the retaliatory strikes on Kuwait and Bahrain.

## The Indian Stakes

More than 4.5 million Indians live in Kuwait, Bahrain and the wider Gulf — the largest concentration of Indian workers anywhere in the world outside India. Kuwait alone is home to roughly 1 million Indians; Bahrain hosts over 400,000.

These are not abstract numbers. They are nurses in Bahrain's Salmaniya Medical Complex, engineers on Kuwait's al-Zour refinery, drivers, shopkeepers, IT workers and teachers who have built lives in the Gulf over decades. For their families back in India, the sound of air-raid sirens in Manama and Kuwait City is not geopolitics — it is a phone call that does not go through.

India's Ministry of External Affairs has not yet issued a fresh advisory for Gulf-based Indians, though the existing one — updated during the initial hostilities in March — urges "utmost caution" and asks citizens to register with the nearest Indian embassy. India operates one of the world's largest consular evacuation capabilities, tested most recently during the 2023 Sudan crisis and the 2015 Yemen operation (Operation Raahat).

## Oil and the Strait

The Strait of Hormuz had just begun to reopen after months of near-total blockade. Hundreds of oil tankers that had been trapped inside the Gulf started moving through the waterway, and oil prices tumbled to pre-war levels — Brent crude ended the week at $72 per barrel, down from highs above $120 during the worst of the fighting.

That recovery is now at risk.

Iran has been asserting control over shipping lanes, demanding vessels use a northern route through Iranian waters and seeking to charge transit fees. Washington has been promoting an alternative southern lane along the coast of Oman. The two approaches are fundamentally incompatible, and the renewed attacks are a signal that Iran views the strait not as a neutral waterway but as sovereign territory.

For India — the world's third-largest oil importer, with roughly 85% of its crude arriving by sea — a re-escalation in the strait is an immediate economic threat. Russia currently supplies more than half of India's oil imports, but the strait remains the transit point for crude from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Kuwait.

## The Lebanon Dimension

The ceasefire's collapse extends beyond the Gulf. Iran accuses the US of violating its commitment to end hostilities in Lebanon, where Israel invaded in March and continues to occupy large swaths of the south. A US-brokered security framework signed on Friday was rejected within 24 hours by Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem, who called it "null and void" and a "surrender."

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz praised the same agreement for allowing Israel to maintain its occupation of a security zone in southern Lebanon and bar displaced residents from returning — a framing that makes any broader peace deal harder, not easier.

## What Comes Next

The Revolutionary Guards have declared that "American bases in the region will experience hell in the coming days." Trump has issued an existential threat against the Iranian state. Neither side appears to have a clear off-ramp.

For the estimated 8.5 million Indians across the Gulf — in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman — the calculus is grimly familiar. They have weathered every Gulf crisis since the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait. They endured the early months of this war. They will likely endure this too.

But every escalation makes the implicit bargain of Gulf migration — economic opportunity in exchange for geopolitical risk — a little harder to accept.
